title: volatile vs Atomic classes (AtomicInteger, AtomicReference, etc.) — when to use each

s1_definition.profdef: Use **volatile** when you only need VISIBILITY — a single variable written by one thread and read by many, with no compound operations (`volatile boolean shutdown`, `volatile Config latestConfig`). Use **Atomic classes** when you need VISIBILITY + ATOMICITY — compound read-modify-write operations on a single variable (`AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`, `AtomicReference.compareAndSet()`). Atomic classes use hardware CAS (Compare-And-Swap) — lock-free, no blocking, no deadlock risk. The Atomic family: `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `AtomicBoolean`, `AtomicReference<V>`, `AtomicIntegerArray`, `LongAdder` (striped for high contention), `AtomicStampedReference` (solves ABA problem).
s1_definition.analogy: **volatile** = a GLASS DISPLAY CASE showing the current gold price. Everyone can SEE the latest price (visibility). But if two traders try to UPDATE the price simultaneously, one update is lost (no atomicity). **Atomic classes** = a MECHANICAL PRICE TICKER that clicks to the next value. Each click is ONE atomic move — two traders clicking simultaneously: both clicks register, neither is lost. The mechanism guarantees one-click-at-a-time at the hardware level.
s1_definition.oneliner: volatile = visibility only (flags, status, one-writer). Atomic = visibility + atomicity (counters, CAS operations, lock-free). volatile for reads, Atomic for read-modify-write.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Use **volatile** when you only need VISIBILITY — a single variable written by one thread and read by many, with no compound operations (`volatile boolean shutdown`, `volatile Config latestConfig`). Use **Atomic classes** when you need VISIBILITY + ATOMICITY — compound read-modify-write operations on a single variable (`AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`, `AtomicReference.compareAndSet()`). Atomic classes use hardware CAS (Compare-And-Swap) — lock-free, no blocking, no deadlock risk. The Atomic family: `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `AtomicBoolean`, `AtomicReference<V>`, `AtomicIntegerArray`, `LongAdder` (striped for high contention), `AtomicStampedReference` (solves ABA problem).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **volatile** = a GLASS DISPLAY CASE showing the current gold price. Everyone can SEE the latest price (visibility). But if two traders try to UPDATE the price simultaneously, one update is lost (no atomicity). **Atomic classes** = a MECHANICAL PRICE TICKER that clicks to the next value. Each click is ONE atomic move — two traders clicking simultaneously: both clicks register, neither is lost. The mechanism guarantees one-click-at-a-time at the hardware level.

**One line to remember:** volatile = visibility only (flags, status, one-writer). Atomic = visibility + atomicity (counters, CAS operations, lock-free). volatile for reads, Atomic for read-modify-write.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The trading service needed five concurrent data points:** (1) Shutdown flag: `running` — one writer (shutdown handler), many readers (worker threads). (2) Trade counter: incremented by 200 threads simultaneously. (3) Latest market price: one feed writer, 100 reader threads. (4) Connection pool initialized flag: one-time CAS from false→true. (5) Active session count: add/subtract by many threads. Solution: (1) `volatile boolean running`. (2) `LongAdder txnCount`. (3) `AtomicReference<Price> latestPrice`. (4) `AtomicBoolean initialized`. (5) `AtomicInteger activeSessions`.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Shutdown flag (`volatile boolean running`): writer sets false → all 200 reader threads see false immediately → loops exit. No Atomic needed — simple read/write, no compound operation.

**Step 2.** Session counter (`AtomicInteger`): 50 threads login (increment) and logout (decrement). CAS ensures every increment/decrement is counted. Final: exactly 0.

**Step 3.** One-time initialization (`AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true)`): 50 threads race to initialize. CAS: only ONE succeeds (the first to CAS false→true). Others see true → skip. Initialized exactly once.

**Step 4.** Market price (`AtomicReference<MarketPrice>`): feed thread creates new immutable Price, CAS-swaps the reference. Readers always see a consistent price (immutable object). No torn reads.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ VOLATILE vs ATOMIC — DECISION TABLE ═══

  USE CASE                          TOOL            WHY
  ───────────────────────────────  ──────────────  ────────────────────
  Shutdown flag (read/write)       volatile         visibility only
  Latest config (ref swap)         volatile         single ref write
  Transaction counter (++)         AtomicInteger    compound: r-m-w
  Active sessions (add/sub)        AtomicInteger    compound: add/sub
  One-time init (CAS)              AtomicBoolean    conditional set
  Price update (immutable swap)    AtomicReference  CAS on reference
  High-throughput counter          LongAdder        striped cells
  Multi-variable update            synchronized     not possible with Atomic!

  ═══ PERFORMANCE (64 threads, 1M ops) ═══
  volatile read:          ~1ns   (fastest, but no atomicity)
  AtomicInteger CAS:      ~10ns  (lock-free, CAS retries)
  LongAdder:              ~2ns   (per-thread cells!)
  synchronized:           ~50ns  (monitor lock, context switch)
```

```
  ═══ HLD — Atomic Primitives in Trading Service ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Trading Service (200 threads)                     │
  │                                                     │
  │  volatile boolean running      ← shutdown flag     │
  │  LongAdder txnCount            ← 50K TPS counter  │
  │  AtomicReference<Price> price  ← market feed       │

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Atomic Class Hierarchy ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  AtomicInteger                     │
  │  - value: volatile int             │
  │  + get(): int                      │  volatile read
  │  + set(int): void                  │  volatile write
  │  + incrementAndGet(): int          │  CAS loop
  │  + compareAndSet(exp, upd): boolean│  single CAS
  │  + getAndUpdate(fn): int           │  CAS + function
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  AtomicReference<V>                │
  │  - value: volatile V               │
  │  + get(): V                        │
  │  + set(V): void                    │
  │  + compareAndSet(exp, upd): boolean│  CAS on reference
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LongAdder                         │
  │  - base: long                      │  for low contention
  │  - cells: Cell[]                   │  for high contention
  │  + increment(): void               │  CAS base or cells[hash]
  │  + sum(): long                     │  base + Σ cells
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  CAS hardware instruction (x86: CMPXCHG):
  if (memory[addr] == expected)
    memory[addr] = newValue; return true;
  else
    return false;  // another thread changed it → retry!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Use volatile when you need VISIBILITY only — a single variable with simple read/write, no compound operations. Shutdown flags (`volatile boolean running`), latest configuration, status strings. Use Atomic classes when you need VISIBILITY + ATOMICITY — compound read-modify-write operations. `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` for counters, `AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet()` for one-time initialization, `AtomicReference.compareAndSet()` for swapping immutable objects. Under high contention (64+ threads): `LongAdder` is 5-10x faster than `AtomicLong` because each thread increments its own cell (striped design).

All Atomic classes use hardware CAS (Compare-And-Swap) — lock-free, no blocking, no deadlock, excellent throughput. But they only work for SINGLE variable operations. For multi-variable invariants or complex compound operations (check-then-act on balance): use `synchronized`. In banking: shutdown flag → volatile. Transaction counter → LongAdder. Market price → AtomicReference<Price>. Pool initialization → AtomicBoolean. Balance debit → synchronized (multi-step compound operation).

---

keyPoints: Use volatile for flags, Atomic for counters
